No, that's a normal GPS module with sub-meter resolution. We need 1-2 centimeters, the keyword is RTK.

Here's UM960: https://witmotion-sensor.com/products/rtk-gps-gnss-modules-centimeter-level-um982-um980-um960

Or Ardusimple micro: https://www.ardusimple.de/product/simplertk2b-micro/

You'll need an RTK antenna as well, for at least dual-band. Like this one (HA-901 or HX-901): https://ebay.us/m/bo9bYP
Both modules have pins (might need to solder them yourself) that fit on the universal board.
To solder them is not the hard part, it is more to solder it to the correct place / pins. 🙂

Not a problem here. Just look at the UM960. You see a pin header with 6 pins, which fit exactly into the 6 holes on the module. There are two rows of holes, but you only need one. And those 6 pins fit exactly into the board.

It's both hardware and software. You'll take an existing mower, exchange some parts (whole mainboard) and add some new parts (rPi, GPS-RTK module, ...). So basically a full brain transplant 🙂 And on that new brain, there's obviously firmware and the rPI has an installation of ROS with various custom packages to implement all the logic. And then there's the web app to control everything. All that software, the replacement mainboard design and everything on it, that's OpenMower.

One bad I did recognized, doesn't look OS specific but wanna mention for the case that you like to fix it before.
If you do an:
1. `sudo openmower update-self` and afterwards an
2. `openmower update-bootloader`, you'll get bootloader 1.1.6 updated but then hang. Also STM32 reset knob doesn't work!

Then, if you reboot (power-cycle), my CM5 with eMMC isn't quick enough to boot-up to do an `openmower update-firmware` before xCore stops bootloader? Guess `openmower update-bootloader` pulls/installs an old bootloader with timeout issue?!

I think I know what the issue is, it's not related to the OS at all.

There is a register which says where the STM32 should boot from on reset. During power down, this gets reset and the bootloader updates it to point to the user program.

if you call `openmower update-bootloader` while the STM32 is executing the user program, this register is apparently not cleared properly which in turn lets the STM32 load from the user programm address after reset (which is why the reset button doesn't work)

`openmower update-bootloader` clears flash and only flashes bootloader, so the address where the user program _should be_ is empty.
Fix is to update the `openocd` call in the `openmower-cli`, temporary fix is to power-off and power-on after calling `openmower update-bootloader`
Sounds reasonable 🤔 ... so fully OS independent and can be fixed later in openmower-cli 👍

My next idea was to make the ExpansionPort in polled I2C but as far as I could see, we can't switch a single I2C to non-DMA.
At last I tried to make the ADC via STM32 registers but that also quickly became hacky beside the fact that I don't like the MCU hardware dependency.

The NMEA messages on `/ll/position/gps/nmea` are generated by the firmware, it's not a pass-through of what the GPS is sending.
It is only used to send back to your NTRIP provider, they need your approximate position to send the corrections from a base station near you. Its expected for the messages to look like this.

The important part is the `/ll/position/gps` where it shows the accuracy and flags. That's where your exact position will show (X/Y in meters, relative to your DATUM point which is set in your yaml config)

How can I be sure that the GPS is using RTK corrections?

The `flags` field in `/ll/position/gps` needs to be `3` for a full RTK fix, if you see `5` (RTK float), the comms to your NTRIP provider are working correctly, but it's an issue with reception. If you see `0` as flags and accuracy is good (around 1 meter), there is probably an issue with communication to your NTRIP provider

Nice idea taking the modular route. That's also basically what we're doing in general. The xESC boards are the same for all motors and mowers (yardforce, sabo, universal, v1 hardware, etc) to cut on cost and make replacement easy. The universal board also has a modular charger board. Maybe you want to look into those schematics, since the charger IC is already implemented in the drivers.

RE your ROS question: OpenMower is open source, you can build the mower without the xCore board. The idea was (similar to the ESCs) to make it a single piece to drop into the build and use the same piece and 95% of firmware for all builds.

If you want to roll your own, you need to implement custom mower comms. We currently have three implementations: `mower_comms_v1` for the old v1 hardware (no xCore board), `mower_comms_v2` for comms via Etherenet to the xCore and there's `mowgli` for directly talking to a firmware on a reversed engineered YardForce board. Basically you'd also do that implementation for your hardware then. You can talk to it however you like (ethernet, UART, USB), in the end you need to provide a piece of software which:
- runs on linux and talks to your hardware however you like
- subscribes to ROS topics (e.g. ROS outputs "go speed X" and you need to send that to your motor controllers)
- publishes to ROS topics (e.g. your hardware measures motor speed and needs to send that to ROS)

The interface itself is not documented, but it's stable and simple. Look at which topics the existing comms are consuming and do the same

Note that if you were to take the xCore route, the v2 firmware is very modular. Each robot has its own robot class and just overrides some basic settings like charge currents and voltages. Then it "just works". Even if you don't use the same charger IC or your motor controllers speak a different protocol than VESC, you can provide driver implementations, it's all made to be extended.

Here are the implementations to look at:
- https://github.com/ClemensElflein/open_mower_ros/tree/main/src/mower_comms_v1
- https://github.com/ClemensElflein/open_mower_ros/tree/main/src/mower_comms_v2
- I won't list Mowgli, since it's outdated and only works with an old version of OpenMower
Hope that helps 🙂

I have checked it, if you have an older version of the OpenMower OS, you need to adapt your `/etc/systemd/system/openmower.service` and `/etc/systemd/system/openmower-debug.service`  files so that they dont try to pull the images with "releases-" prefix.

Mainly this line need to be changed:
`ghcr.io/clemenselflein/open_mower_ros:releases-${OM_VERSION}`
needs to be changed to
`ghcr.io/clemenselflein/open_mower_ros:${OM_VERSION}`

then apply the changes using `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`

(The actual tag is `1.0.2` and the older OS always adds `releases-` to it, so that makes it `releases-v1.0.2` which doesn't exist)

I'm looking into the universal board again and now I remember why I didn't power the logic directly through the docking station (bypass the charger), like its done on the YardForce and Sabo boards:
When the boards are separated, the power connectors to connect them up again are currently the same (V_BATTERY).

If we want to power the logic through the dock without the charger enabled, we'd need a diode to feed that power (otherwise we'd charge the battery by accident). For the ESC power we don't want that diode, since having that diode will prevent breaking current from flowing back into the battery.

This would mean that one of the four power connectors will be different from the others, which makes wiring more complicated. So the question is: shall we do it regardless or just keep as is? @Apehaenger

- should we remove the diode (and replace with a capacitor, on the universal there's already a 22pF cap), or
- change the voltage divider so that it doesn't have as much impact (e.g. 1.3k/20k instead of 13k/200k resistors)

So I tried and did some changes. With the newest bootloader it's like this:
- if(developer mode enabled): wait for dhcp, then 30 seconds wait time, then blindly jump into the user program. This is fine since if you then use `openocd` the reset will directly start in the user program, so you don't have to wait anymore and power-off, power-on gives you enough time to recover in case something goes wrong
- if(!developer mode enabled)
  - if(started_from_power_up): instantly boot into user program
  - if(software_reset): wait for DHCP, then wait 5 additional seconds for bootloader commands to arrive
also the `openmower` tool now can enable/disable developer mode for the bootloader
so with the new version (1.1.9) your firmware should start in <1second after powering on the mower (green heartbeat).

There's an hidden default mower_params.yaml setting, which is:
```
ll:
  services:
    input:
      config_file: /opt/open_mower_ros/src/open_mower/params/hardware_specific/Sabo/inputs.yaml
```
The location is within your docker image. You can't change that file. But you can set your own one within your personal mower_config.yaml!
This is the content of the inputs.yaml within the docker image: https://github.com/ClemensElflein/open_mower_ros/blob/v2/src/open_mower/params/hardware_specific/Sabo/inputs.yaml

We had recently talked about how having the datum helps with some features, especially satellite view and GeoSJON export.

I had initially mixed the datum into the `map/json` payload in `xbot_monitoring`. Then I got rid of that again because it would be cleaner to just pass the map through. But today I thought: What if we put the datum right into the `map.json` on the disk?

The thought behind it: Without the datum, the relative map coordinates are meaningless. I know, with only LiDaR there are no absolute coordinates, but I'd estimate that 100% of us have GPS.

For my app, it's not a big difference whether I pull the datum from the `map/json` or `params/json` topic. I'd want to have the latter anyway, even if it's only for debugging.

Having it inside the map feels a bit nicer because it would bundle all relevant information together. And it enables one other feature: We could check whether the map datum matches the configured datum and warn the user about it (or fix it automatically). Or even take the map's datum for the GPS-to-relative translation, getting rid of the parameters. The datum could be chosen automatically by the first recorded point.

If you ever want to share your map for analysis, it just one line to remove. The app would anyway offer a download button and could let you choose between `map.json`, `map.json` without datum and GeoJSON fornat.

- Dragging points is there, as well as many other editing features.

For the long-term future, I would prefer the recorded outline to be the actual outer coordinates of your lawn, not the mid of the mower during the outermost round. That would make it easier to offset them (differently next to a wall or to another lawn area) and help with turning close to the border (since mowers tend to be no perfect circles).
- Update is live, yes, as soon as you hit save.
- Robot controls: Sure, but for now my focus was on the map editor, as existing options weren't good.
- Siren: Why? And what would make the sound?
- Speed control: Like any other parameters you might want to adjust - sure. But I don't think we have any API for that, so how sure are you that it actually does something?
- Parameter test mode: From what I've seen it looks like you could easily destroy the map there. I assume the existing map is in memory to be restored later? That feature should live in the ROS code, the app would only trigger it. My work for https://discord.com/channels/958476543846412329/1284249259474026559 (neglected for the past months) helps a bit with that, as the `mower_logic` package becomes just the receiver of work to do, it no longer iterates through area by itself. That planning part moves to a new package, and it could send a plan which includes only the outline.
- Undo/redo: Exists (until you save)
- Edge length labels: To be honest, I don't understand why this would be useful. If you need a "measure distance", maybe, but I guess you know your lawn. And it won't work with many curves.
- Rulers: Why not squared? And again, I don't see how this would be useful unless you draw all your routes.

And `params/set_mow_speed` doesn't exist either. `map/json` is only published, but that's not how you update the map. You might see the app picking it up because that's where it expects the map, but it has absolutely no influence on where the mower is driving. The companion script seems to have something to write files, and it looks like it overwrites the `map.json`, but be aware that this requires a restart of the ROS stack.

OpenMower software is an open source project (fully GPL licenced, also the v2 firmware). The hardware consists of some open hardware components (e.g. the OpenMower v1 mainboard, OpenMower v2 mainboards) and some non open hardware (like the Raspberry Pi, GPS module, or, for the v2 hardware, the xcore board).
I think that's where @Apehaenger is pulling the connection, some people are saying "I don't want v2 mainboard, because the xcore is not fully open hardware" but have no problem getting Raspberry Pis and / or other chinese closed source compute models.

So it depends on where you draw the line. If you say "everything must be open hardware" then neither the v1 nor the v2 hardware is for you, if you draw the line at "all modules created by people involved in the open mower project must be open hardware", then the v2 hardware is not for you.

However with v2 you get the easiest way to start, the best performance and you are actively supporting the project. Also when implementing a new carrier on the v2 platform, it is designed to be easily extensible to new mower models. The mainboards are kept simple and the existing ones can be used as a template, so creating a new one is easy. The firmware changes for such an adapted boards are minimal. V1 hardware is still fully supported, but considered legacy

Your other option is to build custom hardware on whatever components you like and implement the comms to your hardware yourself (OpenMower is open source and modular, so you can disable the hardware comms module completely and provide your own).

What currently happens is:

The v2 hardware looks like this:
Motor controllers, GPS, IMU, Charger etc are connected to STM32 (via low level interfaces. UART, SPI etc). The STM32 converts this to higher level signals like "speed" and "position" and sends those out via Ethernet.

On the other side, the Raspberry Pi listens on Ethernet (the actual software is just a docker container). 

So with the v2 hardware as a base, the software does not care, if it's running on a Pi, a Jetson or an x64 PC. It just needs an Ethernet interface to the hardware.


When you add the Pi to your system, you effectively run a whole Pi for a single docker container. You can just start that docker container on your Jetson as well.

In https://github.com/ClemensElflein/open_mower_ros/pull/274, I prepare for smoother position updates, position history (even when the client connects while the mower is already driving) and events meant for humans.

As base technology, I added a generic forwarder where nodes publish to a ROS topic with an MQTT topic, the payload and retain flag, and xbot_monitoring just forwards it to MQTT.

I use that for the events, with some helper functions to easily integrate it where something happens that the end user might want to know about (e.g. high level state changed, area started, emergency set/cleared, GPS lost/restored, blades on/off,...). Some have additional details like the docking or emergency reason (although the latter isn't implemented yet). Expected event interval is minutes, not subseconds, not meant as a debug log. I plan to display this as somewhere so it's easier to see what was going on. It also shall also help me to display the track differently when the blades are off (dotted line). Mower events have coordinates, so they could be displayed on the map (for GPS lost, that might not be meaningful though). The exact events are a first attempt, not fully reviewed.

Position is published more frequently for smoother UI updates, especially in curves. I plan to smoothen the points on the client at regular intervals to avoid huge polygons. The simplified segments would go into a separate map layer/feature, so that the one with frequent updates doesn't become too big.

Both events and position have a history that can be requested via RPC. That part isn't finalized yet. For now, they're stored in unbounded JSONL files. Position is also simplified and stored on the mower at regular intervals and when an event arrives. Would make sense to use the same parameters as in the client.

The transition from historical records to live data is also not 100% clear yet.

@Tektek  and @ow is probably also interested 😉 : I highly increased the data collecting around the Battery stuff. Dock, charger, BMS, Cells, ... It uses now another collecting approach:
Simply start a rosbag recording of the /ll/power topic via this short line you've to fire in `openmower shell` 😇 :
`nohup rosbag record --size=9 --duration=168h --max-splits=2 --output-name="/data/recordings/${HOSTNAME}_ll_power_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).bag" --lz4 /ll/power & echo $! > /tmp/rosbag_power.pid && echo "Started PID $(cat /tmp/rosbag_power.pid)"`
This will record /ll/power in a bag file in `~/recordings` outside the container.
It will record in background how long you like to record. Preferably at least a full mow- as well as charge- session.
When done, stop the recording again via this: `kill $(cat /tmp/rosbag_power.pid) && rm /tmp/rosbag_power.pid && echo "Stopped"` (in openmower sehll again).
Download the bag file to your PC, and then...
Load this HTML in your browser and load the recorded bag into it.

By the way, here's how I set up an NTRIP multiplexer/relay to use the same upstream NTRIP connection (here: SAPOS) for multiple mowers/devices. I have a little Linux server at home on which I set this up.

```
git clone -b rtklib_2.4.3 https://github.com/tomojitakasu/RTKLIB.git
cd RTKLIB/app/consapp/str2str/gcc
make
sudo cp str2str /usr/local/bin/
```

Then created `/etc/systemd/system/ntrip.service`:
```
[Unit]
Description=GPS NTRIP Relay
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
Restart=always
RestartSec=10
ExecStart=str2str -in ntrip://user:pass@www.sapos-bw-ntrip.de:2101/VRS_3_4G_BW -out ntripc://:2101/SAPOS -p 50.1234 9.1234 123.45 -n 5000 -d 30000

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

The `-p` parameter sends a fixed position, so no GGA to the caster required. Might not be necessary if not using VRS. Finally:
```
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now ntrip
sudo systemctl status ntrip
```

I’m currently calibrating a new large mowing area, and I’ve run into the same challenge someof us face. *if the perimeter geometry isn't perfect, the robot often gets stuck or skips edges*, but I only find out at the very end of the task because of the current** Inside → Outside** perimeter order.

I recall the safety of the robot's approach/heading when hitting the boundary, and I completely understand the reasoning. 
However, for those of us mapping large areas, waiting for the inner loops to finish just to check the outer boundary is very time-consuming.

Since a dedicated "*Perimeter Test Mode"* was discussed as a potential solution, I’ve been experimenting a way to implement this as an optional feature that keeps the safety logic intact for normal operation, but allows for quick boundary validation.

**My proposal**
I’ve drafted a way to expose an *outline_out_in parameter *via *dynamic_reconfigure*. When enabled (for testing purposes), it allows the mower to tackle the outer boundary first.

Here is the logic I would like to test (via vibecoding)

**1. Service Definition (PlanPath.srv):**
*C++*
`// ADDED: Flag to allow Out-In perimeter testing
bool outline_out_in`

**2. Configuration (MowerLogic.cfg):**
*Python*
`# ADDED: Exposed for dynamic_reconfigure
gen.add("outline_out_in", bool_t, 0, "Mow outlines from outside to inside (Warning: check boundary approach safety!)", False)`

**3. Planner Logic (coverage_planner.cpp):**
*C++*
/`/ ADDED: Logic to reverse the perimeter processing
if (req.outline_out_in) {
    std::reverse(area_outlines.begin(), area_outlines.end());
}
for (auto &group: area_outlines) {
    // ... existing logic ...
}`

**4. Behavior Integration (MowingBehavior.cpp):**
*C++*
`// ADDED: Pass the parameter to the planner
pathSrv.request.outline_out_in = config.outline_out_in;`

Does this implementation approach seem correct enough to be used as a "test mode"?
I am aware of the concerns regarding the approach angle/safety at the outer boundary. By making this an optional, user-triggered parameter, is possible to considering this for the official codebase?

ISC0703NLS FET looks good, both lower gate charge and resistance than the one I'm using although the voltage rating may not give you a lot of margin (not sure what your battery voltage is?).  Also interesting that the ISC07 actually rated for lower continuous current than the ISC06 despite the lower on resistance; think the reason is the thermal resistance, 2.5C/W on the ISC07 vs 1.2 on the ISC06.  Depends on the heatsinking which will be better in a particular application.  Without any additional heatsinking my guess is that the ISC07 will run cooler on the xEsc.

I found the combination of the smaller shunt and the lower on resistance did help keep the temperatures down (although my currents are a bit lower than yours).  More details on my results are above, just search for  ISC0602NLS.
Only other thing that might help if your battery voltage is high is to use a separate regulator to feed the TMC6200 12V rather than the internal regulator (as suggested by @c.ez somewhere above).

I did find the current noise a little higher than I expected on the Esc but I think it's largely down to the offset/references.  If that is the case then changing to a 5mR shunt may not be too bad noise wise (if shunt/amp noise is less significant than offset noise).

You need to measure the number of ticks for one meter. I most do it that way that I mark a longer way like 10meters. Write down the starting tacho. Manually drive the amount of your marked meters. Record the end- tacho value, divide the number of tacho-tick-difference (start/stop) by the amount of meters your measured. Then you'll get pretty precise "ticks per meter"
then...

enter it in your mower_params `openmower config ros` like this:
```
ll:
  services:
    diff_drive:
      wheel_distance_m: 0.45
      ticks_per_m: 1195.0
```
Also your wheel distance is important if you build a new mower e.g. with a Universal Board

Only when the remote side is offline and queuing is enabled, according to Claude:

---

Yes, Mosquitto bridges do buffer messages when the connection to the remote broker is down, but the behavior depends on configuration.

**Queueing while disconnected**

When a bridge connection drops, Mosquitto queues outgoing messages locally and forwards them once the connection is re-established. Relevant settings:

- `queue_qos0_messages` (default `false`) — whether QoS 0 messages are queued while disconnected. By default they're dropped.
- `max_queued_messages` (default `1000`) — per-client queue limit, applies to the bridge's "client" side.
- `max_inflight_messages` — how many QoS 1/2 messages can be in flight unacknowledged.
- `bridge_max_packet_size` — caps packet size across the bridge.

QoS 1 and 2 messages are queued by default; QoS 0 only if you explicitly enable it.

**Persistence across restarts**

If `persistence true` is set, the queued messages (and retained messages, subscriptions, etc.) survive a broker restart, written to `persistence_file`. Without persistence, the queue is memory-only and lost on restart.

**No intentional delay in normal operation**

When the bridge is connected, there's no artificial batching or delay — messages are forwarded as they arrive. Any latency you'd see is just TCP + TLS + network RTT + broker processing. If you're seeing unexpected delays while the bridge is up, likely suspects are:

- `keepalive_interval` affecting reconnect detection, not throughput
- `restart_timeout` / `idle_timeout` causing reconnect gaps
- TLS handshake on reconnect
- The remote broker being slow to ACK QoS 1/2, which backpressures through `max_inflight_messages`

**Notify topic**

Bridges publish connection state to `$SYS/broker/connection/<bridge_name>/state` (or a custom topic via `notification_topic`), which is useful for detecting when buffering is actually happening.

1. Bridge is the standard way to replicate MQTT messages to/from multiple brokers. The Mosquitto team has surely put more time into optimizing this scenario than we have.
2. Offloading the remote communication (over a potentially weak WiFi connection) to an extra process sounds better to me than handling it in ROS. Sure, I think the MQTT lib does the actual network communication in a separate thread, but IIRC, it can still have an impact on the main process when the queues become too big etc. If ROS just needs to talk to the local broker, that's pretty much guaranteed to work and to be fast.
3. I have something in the pipeline for "meta" commands like restarting the Docker container, reading log files and changing config with my new app. That has to be an extra process outside of ROS, and without a bridge, it would have replicate the same dual-connection logic.
4. It adds some more complexity to our code, although that's neglectible compared to many other things.

That said, I currently also use the external MQTT setting because it's easy. It's not that bad, but especially for point 3 I would rather set up a bridge from the config than reimplement the dual connection logic.

No, AFAIR, the problem was a deadlock with MQTT, where one thread holds the MQTT lock (implicit in the "connected" callback) and wants to get a lock for the sensor data (so it can retrieve and publish it), while a second thread holds the sensor lock (to build the JSON) and wants to get the MQTT lock (to publish it). I think it was even the same method that was called from two threads, once for the "connected" callback from MQTT and again because the ROS subscription published first data.

And the fix for that was to release the sensor data lock before publishing to MQTT by adding an artificial scope around the JSON construction part of the method. That way, the threads might have to wait for one lock or the other, but won't deadlock because the second thread never holds both locks at the same time.

MQTT is only used for the various apps, HA etc.,  not for the mower operations. It makes sense to reduce the data rate for that, in my PR for the position history I already did that (fixed publishing rate every 150ms, rather than almost 50 Hz as "accidently" dictated by the IMU update rate).

But I don't see why an external MQTT would need different update rates than the internal one. Again, both target apps with similar requirements, it's more about remote access, using an existing broker in HA etc.

And sure, Mosquitto needs to take care of the forwarding - but it's guaranteed to never interfere with ROS. Whereas a slow connection to the external MQTT could fill up queues inside xbot_monitoring. Not sure if at some point that would delay/prevent the publishing to the internal MQTT or have other negative consequences - but I feel better if that is complety excluded.

And with the OpenMower service, we would have the dual connection in two places, whereas the bridge would simply take care of everything.

My string analysis of the ESP32 firmware suggests that it contains the high-level commands and overall system logic. In contrast, the Nation chipset appears to handle low-level motor control and likely transmits telemetry data back to the ESP32.

Given this, I question the value of focusing on extracting the main microcontroller firmware. The ESP32 binary already seems to provide everything necessary to communicate with the Nation chipset.

If we were to extract firmware from the Nation chipset as well, we would likely face the same challenge, interpreting low-level assembly code that is difficult to analyze.

Potential Approaches

1. **Replace hardware components**
   Scrap the existing motherboard(s) and purchase new motor controllers and related components.
   * Not preferred due to cost (potentially hundreds of dollars) and wasting existing hardware, especially given that it is flash-unlocked.
   * Additional challenge: identifying compatible motor controllers, especially since the existing motors are unlabeled.

2. **Reverse engineer the ESP32 firmware**
   Focus on analyzing the ESP32 binary, which already appears to contain the high-level logic and communication interface.

3. **Dump and reverse engineer the Nation chipset firmware**
   Likely to involve low-level assembly analysis, making it time-consuming and difficult to extract meaningful insights.

4. **Sniff UART communication**
   Attempt to intercept communication between the ESP32 and the Nation chipset.

   * Challenging to capture the full command set.
   * Triggering all behaviors (e.g., mowing) will require setting up boundary wires, which adds complexity.
   * Telemetry data may also be near impossible to interpret without context.

You probably found the explanation already, but it should be as easy as `git rebase -i origin/main` (or whatever branch you want to rebase onto, might need to `git fetch` before). Then you get a list of commits and can choose what to do with them - in this case, simply delete the lines of the superfluous commits. After save & quit, git will apply the commits one by one, as if you had just done the changes. If you changed something on the same lines as the removed commits, you'll get merge conflicts, which you'll need to resolve, stage the files with `git add` and finally `git rebase --continue`. But ideally, all those commits were independent and the rebase will just run through.

I know there are other OM-compatible models, but I wanted to play it safe. In the end, I decided on the YF Classic 500B because I wanted to try Mowgli's reverse engineering before completely disassembling the mower, just in case I need to easily revert everything if problems arise.

Okay its just a simple write once bit to lock the JTAG config
jtagctrl |= 0x8000 locks the jtagctrl register until reset (maybe even until power cycle, not sure)
I think until power cycle
That also explains why its required to power cycle the CPU after each glitch attempt, otherwise it will stay disabled as writing to that register is locked
And 0x4000 is for enable/disable, thats in that early area of instructions so sending your glitch to where they load the CRP value into R1 (0x1FFF0D78) should enable JTAG
Or maybe not, a reset command over SWD also unlocks it again
Either way, with EMFI it should work

Hey everyone 👋

Newcomer here, still building my OpenMower SABO with the xCore board. I've been reading through this whole discussion and I think I get the frustration on all sides — things break, repos diverge, and it's hard to know what to follow.

But honestly? I don't care so much about which project "wins". And both projects clearly have people putting in serious work — respect to everyone involved. What I care about is ending up with the best possible autonomous mower — ROS2, optional Sensors LiDAR, solid navigation, a great UI — and hardware that doesn't lock me in forever.

From what I can see, MowgliNext is heading in a really exciting direction. 

One thing I also really appreciate on the OpenMower side is the openmower-cli — being able to set up and manage everything through a single clean tool is exactly the kind of experience this community deserves. Combining that kind of simplicity with MowgliNext's stack would be something special. And the dream for me personally? Being able to build a mower completely from scratch — no donor mower needed, just raw components and a great software stack on top.

As someone just getting started, I'd love to hear from people who know this stuff better than I do:

• How important is the move to ROS2 really — is it a nice-to-have or is staying on ROS1 a dead end at this point?
• What's currently the best app for running OpenMower day-to-day — scheduling, monitoring, map editing?
• Where is the active development happening for OpenMower right now — which repo should I actually be watching?
• And the big one: is there any serious interest in making MowgliNext hardware-agnostic through a proper abstraction layer and plugin system — so that xCore, GForce, and DIY builds can all run the same stack?

* wind sensor

The software side is also already quite far along. Area planning and path planning are implemented and currently in testing.

Shunt resistance is set here https://github.com/ClemensElflein/xesc_firmware/blob/release_6_05/hwconf/hw_xesc2.h#L112. Max current limits are here https://github.com/ClemensElflein/xesc_firmware/blob/release_6_05/hwconf/hw_xesc2.h#L259. Limits must not exceed the measurable current range or it will blow the MOSFETs
I upgraded my SA battery to 7S2P by adding the missing cells, 2800mAh cell IIRC so 5.6Ah. BMS did not limit charge current on mine, using ~3A but tried 4A+
`I = 2.5/(5*R)` so for the stock xesc at 33mR max measurable current is `2.5/(5*0.033) = 15.15A`. If you piggyback another set of 33mR in parallel it's `2.5/(5*0.0165) = 30.3A`
Better to just replace the shunts though. I just piggybacked the shunt to test until 5mR 3W shunts arrived.
Power/heat from the shunts is I²R, so for 33mR at 10A that's 3.3W so probably at/over their rating

At 16.5mR shunts can measure twice the current range and will generate half the heat. With active cooling IIRC I ran this up to a 10A battery limit, 20A motor limit, 30A abs max current limit. Works pretty well but temps get high very quickly.
Using 5mR shunts and better MOSFETs now, temps are a lot better

In the original project, we're trying to avoid too many parallel variants. Of course, we keep support for both v1 and v2 hardware, because many people have their existing build and ripping that out to use v2 hardware costs a lot of money. But we support both with the same Docker images from the same branch of the same repo. OSv2 isn't officially marked as stable yet, but realistically we don't recommend anyone to use OSv1 for new installs anymore and encourage users to upgrade via reflash (which only costs some time, not money). We'll keep around legacy Docker images (with nginx and mosquitto baked in) for quite some time because that's what OSv1 needs, but hey, it's still coming from the main branch, just with another Docker file and a little conditional code.

It's very odd to me that there seems to be no discussion between the different developers.  I was under the impression that OpenMower wanted to move to ROS2 at some point anyways and was open to adding more sensors.

From my perspective the low level control is almost entirely orthogonal to the high level software.  Mowgli vs vanilla build is just a question of what computer is translating between the ROS commands and the low level controls.

The thing is... time is limited. Contributions come from mainly three devs, and we focus on the things that we feel are important (which might be very subjective). Yes, ROS2 is a plan, but I feel that it should be driven by someone who knows in depth how all the internals work (or should work, current code is far from perfect in some aspects). I wouldn't agree to be just the "consultant" in a migration effort. That would probably cost me more time than doing it myself. The hard parts are architectural, strategical decisions and giving input on the expected behavior. The "adjust code to changed APIs/patterns" should be fairly easy these days with AI support. If someone with less knowledge about the code did the migration, I'm afraid the hard decisions would still be there, but I'd be telling them what to ask their AI to do and push back on what it came up with, instead of just having the discussion directly myself. It's still fine if someone gives it a try, I might be too pessimistic and/or they might make good calls there we can use as is, but I tend to see them more as exploration than as mergable PR.

Posting my setup here for mowing only when the lawn is dry (including calculating rain accumulation, inferred dew rate, and sunlight based evaporation).  I'm just dumping what I have right now because people are interested, but probably at some point I should properly "package" it.  You also need to create three helper inputs. Also note if you adopt this you will need to replace the weather station source for the weather data.  I used kvtsouth134 since it was closest station to me, but it didn't have cloud cover so I pull that from pirateweather.  Here are all the sensors you will need to find/replace with your own local weather data:

- sensor.kvtsouth134_temperature
- sensor.kvtsouth134_dewpoint
- sensor.kvtsouth134_wind_speed
- sensor.kvtsouth134_uv_index
- sensor.kvtsouth134_precipitation_rate
- sensor.pirateweather_cloud_coverage

I created this list of requirements back when I was searching for a library:
- It is open source (GPL compatible) 
- It is modular (i.e. it is designed to work with arbitrary sensors) 
- It supports 3D motion models 
- It supports vision features 
- It supports self-calibration 
- It works with ROS 
- It uses autodifferentiation (i.e. does not require manual derivative calculations)

This is true, also if you have an RTK receiver that will output raw data, you can do deeper sensor fusion.  Basically, you can use other sensors to help you resolve the integer ambiguity problem, so you can get FIX level measurements without having enough satellites for a FIX, and without even having an RTK base station! It's called TDCP measurements (time difference carrier phase). I only know this because it's one of the example usages of WOLF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.12919

The most important thing is that the sensor fusion can work with the lever arm for the GPS antenna (i.e. that the GPS antenna is NOT at the center of rotation of the robot). OK, I was able to update it! Thanks! 👍

I would say moderately reliable.  The main thing is that the closest weather station might not have rain exactly when you do (I did intend to add some forecast smarts to it possibly at some point...).  It's definitely better than simpler methods like checking whether it's currently raining, or only running during fixed hours.  The main thing is you can tune how conservative you want it to be.  The settings I use may be a little bit aggressive.  Just today it was a complete downpour and the wetness reached the max. Then the sun came out (still a bit cloudy) and in a couple of hours it considered the lawn to be dry again. My deck was mostly dry, but there were still wet spots.  The lawn also had remaining drops of water on it.

The key thing to understand about the parameters is that the lawn wetness is measured in "sunshine" units, which is why there is no sunshine coefficient.  So the "max lawn wetness" value tells the system how much sun is needed to dry a "maximally wet" lawn, the rain coefficient tells you how quickly the rain fills up the wetness, and the dew coefficient tells you how quickly the dew fills up the wetness.  So if you just want to be conservative, you could just double all three parameters and it would calculate "twice as much" sunshine is needed to dry the same amount of water.

My reference is the current implementation with slic3r. With the logic we have there, these things work fairly well:
- Outline is covered by some rounds from inner to outer
- Around obstacles, we also drive some rounds
- For obstacles close to the outline, the rounds are combined into one driving track
- Between the rounds, we have smooth transitions
- For the fill (which may or may not overlap with the outline rounds), it uses parallel lines
- If one mowing area is shaped in a way that it one big fill doesn't work, it automatically creates multiple smaller ones, e.g. from one edge to an obstacle (or a concave part of the outer shape) and then another one from the other side of the obstacle to the other edge
- The lines in all fills have the same angle, which can easily be configured
- Turns between the lines are planned as half-circles
- Navigation between the different paths for outlines and the various fills is not planned, it's done at runtime using a costmap
- The paths are ordered in a fairly sensible way
- The input area is defined as a polygon with wholes, where the border is the middle of the mower, not the actual outermost line of the area (e.g. a wall)

OK, second attempt to write down the things that I think could be better. Generally, I would say most of the described behaviors are desired, but:
- When you have some obstacles, and depending on the angle, there tends to be a bit too much fragmentation, i.e. many separate fill areas. And often enough, these are either narrow stripes which are mowed in a tight zig-zag (so it's constantly rotating) and/or small areas. Especially for the zig-zag, it would probably make sense to relax some of the constraints, especially the same angle everywhere, in order to mow the stripe in a few long, straight lines instead.
- Fragmentation could sometimes be avoided it the mower was allowed to drive over the same spot twice. For example, bend the line to drive around smaller obstacles instead of splitting the fill. This is different from 3D printing (where you'd put too much material) or agriculture (where twice as many seeds/fertilizer can be problematic, and also a big tractor might cause damage if it leaves existing lines). For us, only the distance and time counts, and those are probably net benefits if we can avoid some navigation between fragmented fills and slower driving due to more turns (mower drives faster on straight lines).
- I also see often that the mower wouldn't even have to drive around an obstacle or concave part of the area - it could drive the whole way as straight line if it drove over the previously mowed outlines, but those aren't part of the fill area and therefore considered off-limits.
- In short: It would be good to define the polygon that needs to be covered, but independently use something like the costmap to defined where it's allowed to drive. We don't *need* to mow the outlines again, but it's OK to drive there, although driving very close to the outline should be done only when it's really worth it.
- We could even drive over other areas, although they might not be mowed yet (tall grass -> worse driving) and we might need to turn the blades off.
Robot mow normaly  about 20-25 min or more then fuse flash...

- I think it would make sense to consider the costmap also for the navigation between the paths, as the actual connection might be much longer than the direct one. That could improve path ordering and choosing better splits (not that it would compare different variants AFAIK).
- I sometimes wonder whether it would be more efficient to avoid the half-circle turns by e.g. mowing only every second row, for which we would need a quarter turn, a few cm straight line and then another quarter turn. And when it reaches the last row, drive back, covering the remaining rows in same fashion. Just idea though, it adds some distance to drive, the look would be different and I don't know if it really helps with anything.
- Some mowers drive backwards on turns, just like when you turn around with a car. Our mowers don't, and it would be harder to tell it when it's allowed to do that, but might be worth researching whether it could help.
- I would really like to pass the actual area boundaries and it would consider the (simplified) mower footprint to know what it can cover with that.
- My Worx mower has "cut-to-the-edge", I actually bought it for that, but that means off-centric tool support isn't just a theoretical thing, but is an absolute requirement.

I noticed that charging is limited in the V2 firmware by just one line of code.

`src/services/power_service/power_service.cpp `line 115. If you change 
`success &= charger_->setChargingCurrent(ChargeCurrent.value, false);`
to
`success &= charger_->setChargingCurrent(ChargeCurrent.value, true);`

then the firmware will use the charge_current set in mower_params.yaml.

there are two limits: one set on the hardware and one set by software. the charger will use the smaller of the two values

by changing `false` to `true` you ignore the hardware limit and allow the software to exceed the limit set in hardware.

good question, I doubt it makes sense (neither the inflation nor the resolution).
It's been a long time. As far as I know, we're doing everything on the global costmap, since we don't have sensors like ultrasonic etc. The local costmap was preparation for that.

- I haven't quite understood when the recovery behavior will kick in exactly, is it whenever the FTC cancels due to not being able to follow the carrot (i.e. whenever we would trim and retry)? Or is it also triggered on low GPS / bump sensor / something? I don't see how
- So the costmap is only used to not back out of the mowing area?
- I haven't followed this PR in depth, but it sounds like this is stable (at least stable enough that we can merge into `edge`?); Sorry for the missing followup on my part.

1. The design of the current patch is such that it will trigger exactly when the FTC cancels due to not being able to follow the carrot.  The is implemented through two parts, one which is the standard MBF recovery behaviors, which trigger whenever it fails to reach a *goal*.  The second is when we are in path-following mode.  Since MBF doesn't have a goal just a path, it doesn't handle any recovery for us, so we manually trigger the recovery behaviors (basically mimicing the behavior of MBF in a way that would generalize to any recovery behavior registered).
2. The costmap is only used to not back out of the mowing area.
3. It's been stable for me, but I have been hoping for at least one other person to test the version that we would merge.  If you scroll back you will see earlier attempts to test but they were confounded by issues of being stuck in emergency mode.
I should probably fix the params to match between the global and local costmap as part of this, so we can test it all together.

The way to check if your main board I2C is still working is to listen to the number of chirp on the start of the robot : if the I2C dont work, rhen it cannot detect the IMU and then it's supposed to chirp 10 times.

@glajci I got something for you 🙂

- You can connect the display to the extension port (note 3.3v voltage levels, I'm not sure how you did it for the Pi, your wiring diagram uses 5v logic which should break the Pi's GPIOs)
- **on your raspberry pi:**
  - Run `openmower update-firmware --from-pr 55` to fetch the one with the remote IO
  - then create a python venv and run `pip install "xbot-service-interface-py[shell] @ git+https://github.com/xtech/xbot_framework.git@v0.1.1#subdirectory=xbot_service_interface_py"` (no pypi yet, need to wait for account activation lol)
  - then fetch `https://github.com/xtech/xbot_framework/blob/main/xbot_service_interface_py/examples/gpio.json` and `https://github.com/xtech/xbot_framework/blob/main/xbot_service_interface_py/examples/lcd_hello.py`
  - adapt the GPIO.json file to the GPIOs you are using for your buttons. They are probably different from mine, since I'm using an old development board
  - now you should be able to run `python lcd_hello.py --bind 172.16.78.1` and see output on screen

Yes, proper architecture is my main concern here. On the one hand, we have devs who have contributed a lot, know the codebase and traps in detail and surely have thoughts what needs to be considered for the future. And then we have new devs who are enthusiastic and might have much more time than we do, but still need to figure out how things are working. So for me it would be important to have a place to write down the "boundaries", architecture plans etc. to act as guidelines for implementations by others. That will often involve a chain of thoughts - I do this that way because some steps later I'm planning to do that other thing. @c.ez  I'm having a bit of trouble understanding exactly what all these different parameters are doing (I'm trying to set up mowgli with the latest `open_mower_ros`).

- OM_V2 (true vs false)
- HARDWARE_PLATFORM (1 vs 2)
- OM_LEGACY_CONFIG_MODE (true vs false)
- OM_MOWER (or just MOWER) (CUSTOM vs e.g. Yardforce500)
- openmower_entrypoint.sh vs openmower_entrypoint.legacy.sh

- OM_V2 is not relevant anymore, it's only for the legacy image, the new image doesn't need it
- HARDWARE_PLATFORM is which low level comms module gets loaded (v1 or v2, for the mowgli you'd do OM_NO_COMMS instead and provide your own)
- OM_LEGACY_CONFIG_MODE is if environment settings are used (the old OM_DATUM_LAT etc) vs the new yaml based config
- OM_MOWER (or MOWER) is used for ROS defaults (antenna offset, wheel ticks per meter)
- the legacy entrypoint and dockerfile contain and load everything (mqtt, nginx, the app as a binary) whereas the new image only contains ros - mqtt, nginx and app are separate docker container started using a compose
mower_config.sh is old and the params currently get translated if `OM_LEGACY_CONFIG_MODE` is set, but don't use it for new things

**Quick Parameter Breakdown:**
**`WORKFREQS ALL ALL`**: Enables all available frequencies  across all constellations.
 **`RTKTIMEOUT 5`**: Fast fallback if NTRIP drops (prevents the mower from drifting blindly into boundaries).
 **`ECUTOFF 15`**: Rejects satellites below 15° elevation to minimize multipath interference near walls/trees.
 **`INTERFACEMODE COM3 AUTO AUTO`**: Handles automatic RTCM injection and NMEA output over USB.
 **`LOG COM3 ...`**: Outputs high-frequency NMEA messages (10Hz for GGA/VTG/RMC) needed for the OpenMower parser.

https://www.bynav.com/media/upload/cms_15/UG017_Interface%20Protocol_Bynav.pdf

**2. Rover Integration (OpenMower Motherboard 2.0)**

* **Hardware Connection**: Connect the Bynav directly to the Raspberry Pi / Motherboard USB.
  * *(swap the old MMCX antenna pigtail for the **IPX (U.FL) to SMA pigtail** to connect HA-901 Helix antenna to the **RF1** port of the M20.)
* **Configuration**: 
  *Run: `openmower configure ros` 
  * and set:
  * `protocol`: `"NMEA"`
  * `port`: `/dev/ttyACM0` (or whichever port is assigned to virtual USB)
  * `baud_rate`: `921600`
  * Set `services/gps/port_index` to `8` in `custom_params.yaml` to force the USB connection path.

**3. Base Station Setup (Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W)**

 **Hardware Connection**: Connect the second M20 via USB to the Pi Zero 2 W using an OTG cable.
 **Software**: Use the specific **GNSSOEM/ELT_RTKBase** fork (**not** the standard Stefal's RTKBase, as this fork provides native auto-detection and custom configuration scripts for Bynav/UM98x receivers).
  ````bash
  wget https://github.com/GNSSOEM/ELT_RTKBase/raw/main/install.sh
  chmod +x install.sh

  ```
* **Web UI RTKBase**: Access the interface, select the USB serial port, choose **Bynav** as receiver type, and set surveyed static coordinates to prevent map shifting.

Hello, please in openmower configure ros what exactly do following parameters do?

  automatic_mode: 0
  gps_wait_time: 5.0
  gps_timeout: 5.0
  rain_mode: 0
  rain_delay_minutes: 30
  rain_check_seconds: 20
 

Automatic mode has something to do with continuing to mow after battery is re-charged if docking/charging is forced during mowing due to low battery? 0 means that I have to click Start manually, so what do I need so that mower continues on its own when battery is re-charged? Otherwise I do not want automatic mowing at given time every day, I use home assistant to start the mower according to weather

gps_wait_time and gps_timeout how to use them? I have part of garden with problematic signal where mower often gets stuck.

rain_mode rain_delay and rain_check how they work with the integrated rain sensor? If rain is detected, the mower gets paused on current position, or is docked? When the water dries from the sensor, the mower will auto-continue or it waits for me to push the button again?

Thank you!!

Automatic mode 0 means you have to manually start it, also after it has recharged. 
1 means you have to manually start it but it will start again after/if it needs to dock to charge. 
2 is auto, which means it will keep mowing 24/7. Will only stop to recharge. 

gps_wait_time I'm not 100% sure what it does, but gps_timeout is how long the mower can loose GPS fix and still mow with the data it already has. Useful when mowing close to walls or trees to keep the GPS fix. The longer timeout you set, the less accurate it becomes and you risk going off course.

Rain delay is exacly as you described. The mower will dock if rain is detected on the rain sensor and start again when it senses no moisture on the sensor. I my experience I've found the sensor to be inaccurate at best and totally worthless sometimes.

Hope that helps.

what you can try without a scope is:
- power the board off and remove the ESC
- measure if either of the tx/rx pins is shorted
  - to GND
  - shorted to 3.3V or 5V
  -  or shorted between each other (TX to RX)

3.3V, GND and 5V you can find on the extension header (screenshot follows)

other than that you can 
- have a look at the trace from tx/rx if it's broken somewhere (mechanically scratched or something obvious)
- have a look at the soldering of the pin sockets of the ESCs, if it looks suspicious (can also share pictures)
in case nothing suspicious turns up, sending it back is the best option (and if you don't want to go troubleshooting, you can also choose to just send it back)

What's important: ROS, app and firmware versions all need to match. I've added things like satellite count and GNSS PDOP, and while I synced it back with upstream, the new BMS battery stuff shifted the definition IDs – so if versions are out of sync, things will break.

Here are the current latest dev versions if you want to try – but be careful if you don't know exactly what you're doing, because I don't either 😅
```yaml
open_mower_ros:
  image: ghcr.io/oe7set/open_mower_ros:1.2.26-dev
app:
  image: ghcr.io/oe7set/openmower-app:0.4.37-dev
```
**FW:**
```
openmower update-firmware --repo oe7set/fw-openmower-v2 --tag v0.0.8-dev
```
Note: FW updates via CLI currently only work with this CLI fork:
```

Problem solved! 

The issue:
After building a new 7S3P pack (Samsung INR18650-35E), the BMS kept shutting off during charging in the docking station. The pack voltage was fine (cells cold, ~28-29V at B+ to B-) but the BMS output was dead after every charging attempt.

The diagnosis:
Following cez's advice, I measured the docking station output voltage directly at the charging contacts — 29.6V unloaded. That's above the maximum for a 7S pack (29.4V) and the BMS was correctly shutting off to protect the cells.

What i did:

Confirmed BMS works perfectly using a bench power supply at 29.0V, charged from 2.3A down to 0.03A without shutting off
Adjusted the DCDC module poti in the docking station from 29.6V → 29.0V
Put the mower back in the station

The result:
Pack now charges perfectly in the docking station — 29.43V, 0.03A, all temps at 25°C, BMS stays on throughout!

I think I've got it figured out.  I analyzed a dozen different examples of the reversal behavior, and I think basically everything boils down to off-by-one timing issues.  The firmware correctly tries to reset the ticks to zero when the direction switches, and when the speed changes from 0 to nonzero.  HOWEVER, both of those resets could happen off by one frame.

Here is an image where the left ticks are reset to 0 the frame *before* the left speed becomes nonzero.  The current code interprets this as a spike  (Note it's not a big enough spike to trigger the workaround 0.6m/s speed limit filter!)

Here is an image where everything works perfectly, where the ticks are reset to zero precisely when the direction reverse, and then reset to zero a second time when the speed becomes nonzero for the left and right wheel respectively

And here is an example where the direction change is broken.  The ticks don't drop until the frame *after* the direction reverses.  So we get two errors here, one that looks like a huge jump up in ticks, and the other that looks like a huge jump down in ticks (but due to abs(), they both become positive)

On my setup, INTERFACEMODE COM3 AUTO AUTO was required to make the module _listen_ to the RTK stream on the right port.

port: " /dev/serial/by-id/usb-1a86_USB_Serial-if00-port0"
    baud_rate: 115200

However, I changed all four parameters to look like this, and this is now the setup that works for me:

      port: "/dev/serial/by-id/usb-1a86_USB_Serial-if00-port0"
      serial_port: /dev/ttyUSB0
      baud_rate: 115200

https://github.com/ClemensElflein/open_mower_ros/compare/main...jeremysalwen:open_mower_ros:main

Basically:
> - nonlinear_angular_control:  @Pete_MI632 's patch to make the angular control less agressive when you are too far off track
> - velocity_lookahead: @Pete_MI632 's patch to try to accelerate and decelerate slowly (I disabled this since it wasn't working great for me)
> - speed_limiter: @Pete_MI632 's patch to limit the speed the mower movers based on the RPM of the blade (very good to stop the mower from continuing to drive while the blade is spinning up)
> - persistence: @Pete_MI632 's patch to remember paths the mower traveled before and avoid passing over the same spot.
> - recovery_lookahead: my Backward/Forward recovery behavior to try to regain traction when stuck  (see the dev thread) .
> - The aforementioned ChargeCtrlSrv service that I don't use but you might.

dtoverlay=uart1
dtoverlay=uart2
dtoverlay=uart3
dtoverlay=uart4
dtoverlay=uart5`

The recording could be started with this short and simple command in `openmower shell`:

`nohup rosbag record --size=9 --duration=168h --max-splits=2 --output-name="/data/recordings/${HOSTNAME}_ll_mower_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).bag" --lz4 /ll/mower_status /ll/power & echo $! > /tmp/rosbag_mower.pid && echo "Started PID $(cat /tmp/rosbag_mower.pid)"`

It runs `nohup` so you can leave the shell afterwards and also exit the SSH connection. It will record only 2 topics and should not fill up your SD with more than 5-10 MB and will also rotate.

Once you completed a mow session, go again into the `openmower shell` and stop the background recording via: `kill $(cat /tmp/rosbag_mower.pid) && rm /tmp/rosbag_mower.pid && echo "Stopped"`.
Afterwards you'll find a `/home/openmower/recordings/<mowername>_mower_<timestamp>.bag` in which I'm interested in to compare with my own recordings of my "xESC2-Power" Variant.

A patch from @Pete_MI632 , this time a small one, to improve the PID control of the mower.

Basically, we reduce the strength of the angular PID terms when the lateral distance is large.  So effectively you can have good angular control when on the track, but you can still have responsive lateral control when you have wandered away from the track.

The formula is pretty straightforward, it just linearly scales down the strength of the angular PID terms from 100% at 0.0m of lateral error, to 10% at 9cm of lateral error, and beyond 9cm it remains at 10% strength. The `lateral_priority_distance` configures this 9cm distance*.  You can also disable this features entirely by setting `lateral_priority_distance` to `0`.  

I have been running with this setting for the past year or so, and it works well.  Anyone who is running my Mowgli-docker setup (see https://discord.com/channels/958476543846412329/1002292884726362132/1517234071141351575) and of course @Pete_MI632  has tested this patch as well.

*Technically you are configuring the point at which it would reach 0% strength, but due to a minimal strength of 10%, once you are 90% of the way to your `lateral_priority_distance` you will reach the minimal strength.

The velocity lookahead works by trying to work out what the maximum linear speed can be at any point while ensuring that the mower can make it around corners without exceeding the maximum rotational velocity.  It also makes sure there is enough time slow down for a corner if needed without exceeding the set deceleration limit.  

Thinking about it that does rely on the linear speed commanded being pretty close to reality (which it is on mine) and I'm not sure whether that will be the case on all builds.  If it's out then I can see the velocity lookahead giving some unpredictable behavior.

It also relies on the maximum angular and linear velocities, and the acceleration/deceleration limit, being set to realistic values.  If the mower can't actually manage to change speed or direction as quickly as set in the parameters then that will also break the lookahead calculations!

There are three repositories I have

1. My open_mower_ros fork, which mostly has improvements that apply to *any* OpenMower mower: https://github.com/jeremysalwen/open_mower_ros  I am working on getting patches upstreamed one at a time. Many of the patches are originally from @Pete_MI632 . There is also one mowgli-specific patch, but it is just for the charge control service, which I have never used and I think most people won't find necessary.
2. My mowgli-docker fork, which makes mowgli-docker more compatible with the upstream openmower https://github.com/jeremysalwen/mowgli-docker.  Previously, you needed to build separate mowgli-docker docker images, but now that is no longer necessary, you can just use regular open_mower_ros images.  By default it uses my open_mower_ros images, but you could easily point it at ClemensElflein/open_mower_ros instead.  In fact,  my goal is that you won't even need a special mowgli-docker repo eventually, you could just use regular OpenMowerOS in most cases.
3. My Mowgli firmware fork, which has mowgli-specific bugfixes/improvements: https://github.com/jeremysalwen/mowgli There are also message definition updates to work with the latest OpenMower.

If you want to run OpenMower+Mowgli, you really want to get #3, but of IMO all three together provide the best experience.  Just be aware that you are testing some experimental code, that right now only me and @Riho have tested.  

I would be happy to merge these Mowgli-specific changes as well, but it seems like @Cedric isn't active any more with Mowgli development and has moved on to Mowglinext.  I intend to keep OpenMower+Mowgli working regardless, so if people want to use my repository that is also welcome.

This is how mine looks in the most simple case.

But actually, it's much more sophisticated. The driven track is persisted on ROS side, so it survives restarts and you can look at older runs. I introduced a notion of "jobs" and "sessions", where a "session" is from undock to dock (usually - it also considers other idle state) and a "job" is one round of covering all areas, so potentially several sessions with recharging. Tracks are saved as one .jsonl file per job, so that file will usually include each area once. When the next job starts (i.e. starting to mow again after last area was mowed), a new file is started and the map starts blank again.

The tracks are simplified/compacted to reduce the number of points, there's a buffer of "live" points which haven't been compacted yet, which also helps to rerender only a small portion of the track, not all points for every frame.
The backend has a median filter so I take one point every 150 ms, avoiding some jumping around.
The segments in the track are also timestamped, just in case we want to show only a certain part of the track in the future.

Furthermore, I events meant for humans (not technical logs). They help to see why the mower went docking for example. Also persistence here, one file per day. Events are automatically annotated with timestamp, position, job id, session id and position, so we could show them on the map in the future - or for example show the last few seconds of track before an emergency event.

The events will be extended in the future, e.g. I would like to see more details about why an emergency was triggered. I started working on that, but realized that the current architecture of mower_logic makes that not so easy, so I decided to wait until I have rewritten it (no promises though 😅 ).

Also, we might not want to see all events by default - blades on and off is mainly a vehicle to enable the dashed lines in the screenshot above, and GPS turning off and on during (un)dock is also noisy.

Again, the events list isn't super-polished, although Claude Design didn't make better suggestions... and the events are to be extended and fine-tuned. But the hard part - the framework and persistence and everything - is done.

There are various settings involved in the angle calculation. Assuming you keep mow_angle_offset_is_absolute=false (default), then indeed the "base angle" is determined from the area's first straight part. This is the angle that you override with the setting.

Added to that is the mow_angle_offset. If you set that to 90, it you'll have a 90° rotation of your tracks, but you'll notice that this isn't the same angle for all your areas, because their base angle might be different.
And then you have the mow_angle_increment, which increases the angle after each "job" (one full cycle through all areas).
So basically, we have: angle = base angle + mow_angle_offset + (num_finished_jobs * mow_angle_increment)
And again, the base angle is usually derived from the area outline or can now be overridden.
Just for completeness, with mow_angle_offset_is_absolute=true, I think it's: angle = mow_angle_offset + (num_finished_jobs * mow_angle_increment)

My suggestion would be:
- create local costmap, add blobs for detected ultrasonic obstacles
- if the mow path crosses a blob, cut it and run the navigation to wherever the path leaves the blob again
- navigation will then navigate there
- resume path following

Is the 12V fan header controllable from RPI? For example to run always when charging and otherwise based on ESC temp or something like that
I tried to do quick GPIO sweep for some reason I was not able to find correct pin if it's controllable

no, it's an STM32 GPIO. The hardware architecture is deliberately designed in such a way that the Pi is only connected to the low level via Ethernet. You can make it available through the power service for example, and then you can toggle it in ROS.

Background why it's like that:
This allows us to swap the CM4 for CM5 or other compute modules (or external PC) without having issues. On the old revision we were hard-locked to the Raspberry Pi 4 for that reason (no orange banana / whatever pi clone / pi 3 / pi 5, because we needed the UARTs available and at the correct location on the pin header). Also development was a pain because with hardware UARTs on linux you couldn't just plug the board into your desktop PC and run/debug the firmware. Now you can plug whatever linux machine you want via ethernet and run the ROS container and it works.

content: This is the behaviour i've been seeing. Anyone else seen this before?

I have a question about the FTC planner driving behavior.

On uneven and sometimes wet ground, the mower frequently performs in-place rotations. This causes the wheels to slip, dig into the ground and eventually get stuck. If the mower ends up with its front against an obstacle, it still seems to prefer rotating on the spot instead of backing up and trying another approach.

Is this the expected behavior of the FTC planner?

Would enabling forward_only: false help, or is there another recommended way to reduce in-place turns? Ideally, I'd like the mower to make more arc-like turns while moving, using reverse when appropriate, instead of pivoting on the spot whenever possible.

Has anyone tuned the planner successfully for uneven or slippery terrain?

Both of my mowers (C500 and 500B) have broke down in the past week. They have both stopped charging. There is a short on the charging input pins and I have located that Q4 is the problem. I saw that there were some problems in the past with this. Both my boards have PJQ5866A and I have now ordered BSC155N06NDATMA1 instead. It is a bit concerning that they were working fine up to now, where they now have the same problem. Motherboard are also different, 6.0 and 6.1. Urgh, I'm in trouble. Opened the mower up and the battery pack connector and main board power connector were a little close to the GPS antenna connector so I shifted it a little bit in the hope that it might reduce any potential interference. Was successful with that but when I power the unit on I get nothing. I'm reading over 27V at the below (between red and black) but the Pi and ublox don't power up. Help!

for me it was enough to re-check the cables
Very, very odd. Removed power connector from board just to check voltages on the terminals, all looked good and when I plugged it back in, unit fired up

Ok, so shifting that power connector a bit doesn't appear to have corrected the problem. I'm seeing behaviour that I've never seen before. From being Docked if I hit Start, it backs out, but attempts to go further than it ever did before and then goes into a loop of forward/backward movement and then goes into idle mode. Here's a video of what I mean.
This is accompanied by the log getting flooded with messages, like this;
it's a positioning issue, the mower is outside of your map boundaries where it refuses to drive. Is there a nagivation area in front of your dock? If not you need to add one

Carried it to the dock, rebooted and sent it out to mow, it *appears* to be working, for now, hasn't dropped it's RTK Fixed status yet.

Right, yeah, i understand that part, my "feeling" was, since i changed the battery pack at the weekend that the GPS accuracy just fell off a cliff, because before that mod, it mowed pretty much flawlessly for about 2-3 months.

When i opened it up this morning, the connector between the battery pack and the board plug were very close to the GPS antenna connector on the UBlox board, so i ended up shifting that as far away as i could from there and re-assembled.

Since i got it back mowing, it hasn't lost its fixed positioning once and it's been running solid for the last hour or so.

Took a pic when I opened it up, it's pretty close
Had also wondered, *could* the UBlox board be situated under the antenna shield and a ribbon cable of some kind to connect it back to the main board? Probably a daft idea
yes, nothing against that. I don't think you'll gain much from it though
Fair enough, only a thought

Does anyone actually use a custom footprint in the costmap? I noticed footprint is empty and robot_radius is 0.0 in the default configuration. Is the recommended approach to define the mower footprint, or is the planner expected to work correctly without it?

we're inflating the obstacles and check for collision with robot's center point instead of using the actual footprint. This assumes a circular robot

It's good enough for path planning, but not perfectly accurate for obstacle avoidance etc
Thanks, that clarifies it. Which parameter you would increase for the obstacle expansion — inflation_radius, cost_scaling_factor, or both?
what's your goal? I think you are turning the wrong parameter in general

My goal is to stop the mower’s front end from hitting obstacles when it turns near them.

The mower usually follows the planned path correctly with its wheel center, but because the body extends further forward than the assumed circular robot model, the nose can still clip an obstacle during in-place turns.

I’m not trying to fix GPS positioning or the recorded boundary. I’m looking for the correct parameter or method to make the planner keep a little more clearance from obstacles specifically during turns.

Would you recommend changing obstacle inflation, outline offset, or something else entirely?

inflating the obstacles won't fix that. The **mowing** path following doesn't care bout the obstacles and the path planning also doesn't do it

If it happens during "fill" and not during outline (which sounds like what you are describing) then increasing outline_count will be what you want

Edit: Only dynamic navigation paths are affacted by the obstacle inflation, so navigation to the dock etc
this adds an additional outline, so gives your mower more space to turn

I finally managed to get it working. I did a lot and came to a conclusion that:
sudo iptables -F
sudo iptables -X
sudo iptables -t nat -F
sudo iptables -t nat -X
and then a restart of the podman container fixed it...until I rebooted it. So in the end I changed   the line 
--publish 3000:3000/tcp \
to 
--network host \
to bind it to the local host network and that did the trick.

Hi, cool a custom carrier board! As Apeheanger said, you need to program the EEPROM otherwise the firmware refuses to start up.

There are two ways: Program it as `hw-openmower-universal`, if it's pin compatible with the Universal board, you can do it. Then the firmware will start up as it would on the universal board.

If it's not compatible and / or needs drivers loaded first (e.g. you have a display or something with a custom driver) you can give it your own ID and have a custom startup routine / pinout / whatever.

In the 2nd case we'll accept the new board ID and merge it upstream if you are willing to share with others (otherwise we'll have board IDs on there which noone can really use). If not, you can fork the firmware and set your repo URL in the `openmower-cli` tool such that it fetches your fork instead.

Anyways here is the "tool", you need to hard-code the ID and board version, it's not very professional, but it works 😅

I think I used these:
```
RTKTYPE ROVER
SAVECONFIG
FRESET
SERIALCONFIG COM1 460800
UNLOGALL
LOG COM1 GPGSV ONTIME 1
LOG COM1 GPRMC ONTIME 1
LOG COM1 GPGSA ONTIME 1
LOG COM1 GPVTG ONTIME 1
LOG COM1 GPGST ONTIME 1
LOG COM1 GPGGA ONTIME 0.1
RTKTIMEOUT 5
SAVECONFIG
```

Baudrate as you like... some have used 921600 successfully, I just had 460800 with my old GPS and kept it. 

`RTKTIMEOUT 5` means that the fix will be discarded if no NTRIP data arrives for 5 seconds (e.g. bad Wifi). I prefer that for a pretty small, cornered garden. If you have a big free space to mow, you might want a much higher value to let it keep driving until it reaches better Wifi again.

Hello everyone 🙂 For the first time I recorded and mowed an area and some basic questions and problems came up.

1. While charging in the docking station the app shows no GPS. Is this by design? If yes, can I stop it from logging “GPS timeout” and “Low quality GPS” every second?

2. When undocking, the robot drives 3 m backwards and leaves the recorded area until it gets stuck under a tree. Then it “Failed to get a plan”. Are more than 3 m normal?

3. After two laps around the perimeter it starts to mow line by line. At one point on the map, when turning at the end of the line, the mower’s front sways out of the boundary an hits an obstacle. Is it common to have such a problem in a few situations or does this point to a bad configuration?

4. The app shows a mower speed of -1500 rpm in the red range. Is this normal?

5. On a second try the mower motor turned on approx. 5 minutes after mowing had started. It did not turn on when the log said:
open_mower_ros  | [WARN] [1785172610.325155287]: #### om_mower_logic: setMowerEnabled(1, 0) call
open_mower_ros  | [WARN] [1785172610.328638517]: #### om_mower_logic: setMowerEnabled(1, 0) call completed within 0.00348088s
Can I change the log format to a human readable time?

6. The robot finishes near the docking station (A), drives in front of it (B) and when turns again to face towards it, it’s front sways out of the boundary and crashes. Should I relocate the docking station?

Thanks for any advice.

Hi! Sounds like it's just some settings that should fix things for you.
1. Yes, during docking GPS is off, the log spam is a known issue, but it's expected
2. You can set the undock distance in `openmower configure ros` (there should be something like `undock_distance` in `mower_logic`, otherwise: https://openmower.de/latest/docs/knowledge-base/configuration/configure-ros-parameters/)
3. It's a known issue, the default `outline_count` parameter is one too low, so sometimes it hits obstacles while turning. Increasing `outline_count` by one or two will fix it
4. Yes, that's normal. The blue (flutter) app is in maintenence mode, because a new one is being developed (you can already test it: https://github.com/xtech/openmower-app), but since the new app has not yet reached feature parity, it's not the default.
5. have you configured the motor parameters yourself or have you used the provided ones? If you have used the provided ones, you need to turn the mower off and on once (real power up) so that the ESC re-initializes. If you have done that, then doing a motor detection like here should help: https://openmower.de/latest/docs/knowledge-base/configuration/configure-xesc/
6. is there a wall to the `B` point of the lawn? if not, try adding a navigation area to the right. When navigating so close to the boundary, it prefers to stay as close to the lawn as possible, maybe that's the behavior you are seeing

The symptoms were sudden disconnects, sometimes not reconnecting for hours. Even more problematic was that ARP lookup was broken sometimes. This leads to the symptom, that some IPs (e.g. the ntrip server) aren't reachable from the mower, but work fine from other machines.

yes, the OS is just installation convenience, you only need what's in the docker containers. The existing ROS isn't going to help you because it doesn't run the OpenMower nodes. ROS is more of a framework than an OS, so having ROS running already doesn't help you much.

In addition you will need to implement a node that translates what ROS wants the physical robot to do into actual signals to wheels and sensor values back to ROS. There are two levels where you can implement it: on the ROS layer or on an abstraction I built exactly for that task called `xbot_framework` (which I would highly recommend, since I spent a lot of time adding this).

Benefit of using the framework is:
- it's also used in the openmower firmware as well as the mower simulation to talk to the ROS stack, so for the ROS your robot looks exactly like the others.
- it's completely decoupled from ROS, so you can implement this as a plain c++ project
- the interface is clearly defined (https://github.com/xtech/definitions-open-mower)
- you won't need to rewrite your hardware-specific code as soon as we migrate to ROS2, because it doesn't depend on ROS at all

Look at the definitions linked above, and the mower_simulation's implementation of the services (https://github.com/ClemensElflein/open_mower_ros/tree/main/src/mower_simulation/src/services) as well as the firmware implementation of the services (https://github.com/xtech/fw-openmower-v2/tree/main/src/services) and you will see that it's quite straight forward to do it. Also worth checking out the readme here: https://github.com/xtech/xbot_framework/, there's also an example project with example service to get you started.
Of course you don't need to run docker, it's just easier for us to deploy updates like that
