Why not do the following, if you want to get started quickly:
- Create a repo for your GOAT
- Create a ROS noetic workspace in your repo
- add open_mower_ros as submodule, so you get the upstream OpenMower sources and message definitions etc
- add Ecovac's .msg files to the workspace
- add Ecovac's hardware blob to the repo (optional)
- write a small node (python / c++ doesn't matter) which translates from OpenMower's hardware topics to Ecovac's topics. I.e. for each OpenMower message put a subscriber which gets a message and sends Ecovac's message out and vice versa
- compile the ROS workspace, catkin can exclude packages you don't need (e.g. simulation, upstream mower_comms, but that just saves a bit of disk space in the end)
- copy the binaries to the mower and run it

This is better in the long run, because this way you don't have to touch upstream sources at all. If you fork open_mower_ros directly and change the topic structure to use EcoVac's message definitions, you will need to touch all kinds of nodes (positioning, logic, monitoring, etc).

Had to ask Opus:

Mostly true, with one big caveat: it works well at speed, badly at a standstill.

**Back-EMF sensing** (the common method): with three wires and six-step commutation, only two phases carry current at a time. The controller measures the voltage on the floating third phase, where the spinning magnets induce a voltage, and watches for the zero-crossing to time the next commutation. Cheap, no extra wires, works great — but the signal is proportional to speed, so at zero RPM there's nothing to read. That's why sensorless motors start with a blind open-loop ramp, and why they sometimes stutter, twitch backwards, or stall under load on startup.

**Inductance/saliency methods** (HFI, pulse injection): these do give real position at standstill. The controller injects short pulses or a high-frequency signal and measures how fast current rises in each phase — inductance varies with rotor angle because the magnets partly saturate the stator iron. This needs proper current sensing and FOC, and it works much better on interior-magnet rotors than surface-magnet ones. VESC's HFI is the accessible example.

For a lawn robot it matters which motor you mean. A blade motor is an ideal sensorless case: spin up unloaded, then run fast and steady. Drive wheels are the hard case — you want torque from zero, slow precise turns, reversing, and holding on a slope, all of which are where back-EMF sensing is weakest. That's why wheel motors usually have hall sensors (five extra wires) or are brushed gearmotors. If yours has genuinely only three wires and drives a wheel, either it's relying on HFI or the gearbox reduction is hiding a lot of sins.

just a heads up so that you don't struggle when you hit this issue: We're working on merging the OpenMower firmware for all mowers into a single binary, so there will be a `MetaService` which you also need to implement.

The MetaService says which firmware the user has configured (e.g. if one uses the universal board, the hardware alone cannot know all settings), but you can just ignore that. Some mainboards also ignore it, if the board ID already uniquely identifies the actual robot it's running on.

But the MetaService also asks for a "major firmware version" which we'll increment whenever something major breaks and we don't want to have new ROS talk with outdated firmware (should be seldom, since we usually add new things to the services with optional fields etc).

So you will need to add the MetaService and return as MajorVersion the correct magic number for the first release. With the current open_mower_ros that's not an issue yet.

These are NMEA 0183 sentences plus proprietary receiver messages from a GPS/RTK receiver:

**`$GPRMC`** — Recommended Minimum data:
- `131440.00` = UTC time HHMMSS.mmm (13:14:40.00)
- `A` = valid position fix (V would be invalid)
[redacted]
- `0.012` = speed in knots; `202.9` = course/heading in degrees
- `190826` = date 19 Aug 2026; `0.0` = magnetic variation; `E` = easterly variation; `A` = mode A (autonomous)

**`$GPGGA`** — GPS fix data:
- `131440.10` = time
- lat/lon again (slightly different because it's the next measurement epoch)
- `1` = fix type (1 = GPS fix, 0 = invalid)
- `24` = number of satellites in use
- `0.7` = HDOP (horizontal dilution of precision)
- `289.161,M` = altitude above mean sea level (meters)
- `53.660,M` = height of geoid above ellipsoid

**`#BESTPOSA`** — NovAtel (Septentrio/Novatel) proprietary solution message:
- `COM1` = port; `0` = solution sequence; `99.9` = percent of time the solution is computed
- `FINESTEERING` = solution type; `2432` = message ID
- `306898.100` = GPS time of week (ms)
- `SOL_COMPUTED` = solution status; `SINGLE` = solution type (single-frequency, not RTK-fixed)
[redacted]
- `289.1612,53.6600` = altitude & geoid height; `WGS84` = datum
- `0.2718,0.1733,0.3426` = position standard deviations (meters) in N/E/Up
- `0.000,0.011` = velocity, heading; `30,24,24,24` = satellite counts; `00,00,30,37` = age/range

**`$SYSRTS`** — a proprietary/system status message (this format appears to be from the robot/system firmware):
- `306898.00,131440.00` = time stamps
- `53,AT` = status/state; `40,76` = values (e.g. battery/levels)
- `1,1,30` = flags/counts
- `0.000,0.000` = measurements; `59.016` = a value
- `M,Robot` = mode/robot identifier
- trailing numbers = counters/status flags; `*16` = checksum
```

Update: charging is working now.

IC2 is marked **0106**, so it is the correct TSC101CILT and not the wrong INA180 mentioned in the errata.

I also tested `/mower_logic/ignore_charging_current = true`, but this made no difference — there was still essentially 0 A going into the battery.

ROS `/ll/power` showed:

* `charger_enabled: True`
* charge voltage ~29.3 V
* battery voltage ~24.4 V
* charge current ~0.02 A

So software was enabling the charger, but the battery was not actually receiving current.

I then started measuring around **Q6/Q5 and its gate drive circuit**. Q6 initially had ~28.6 V on both outer pins while charging was enabled, so it appeared not to be switching on.

While checking Q5/Q6 again, charging suddenly started working normally. OpenMower now shows about:

* Battery: **25.1 V**
* Charge voltage: **26.2 V**
* Charge current: **0.89 A**

Yes, that's exact the intended behavior. Keep in mind that all three sensor types like stop, lift as well as collision are not forward-looking sensors. Instead of, they get triggered because something already happen.
In your case, it already collided with something, eg. your dog or baby. Driving backward then and try again, could make more damage then the first collision.
You can mitigate the lift and collision sensors by giving it a long delay, like the default 2.5 seconds for the lift sensor... which means: He'll drive 2.5 seconds with one wheel over your pool border, but as soon as a second lift sensor triggers, emergency get immediately happen. Same is for the collision sensors. One may trigger for delay time before an emergency get latched, but as soon two collision sensors trigger, emergency is latched immediately.
